idiom_name: framework router endpoint (Spring Integration @Router, or Apache Camel choice())
implementation_notes: Spring Integration makes the pattern a first-class component: a router endpoint whose method (annotated @Router, or declared with IntegrationFlow.route(...)) receives the message and returns the channel name - or names - to forward to, with AbstractMessageRouter/AbstractMappingMessageRouter as the extensible base classes and SpEL expressions as the compact form for simple conditions. The framework supplies what the hand-written structure would otherwise need (channel resolution, error handling, the default output channel), so the router's content is only the routing rules; Apache Camel's choice()/when()/otherwise() DSL is the equivalent in route-builder form. Delegate to a POJO as soon as a condition needs domain logic, and declare a default output channel so unmatched messages go somewhere visible instead of raising a routing exception.
pitfalls: Returning null, or a channel name that does not resolve to a bean, fails the message at runtime with a routing exception - the framework cannot prove at compile time that every route target exists.
SpEL conditions are strings evaluated per message: renaming a header or payload field breaks them only for the messages that reach that branch, so keep non-trivial conditions in testable Java.
A router endpoint must not transform the message; if it also enriches or converts, downstream endpoints see a payload the flow's published contract never promised.

variants.name: Broker-side JMS message selector
variants.idiom_name: MessageConsumer created with a message selector
variants.implementation_notes: JMS implements the pattern as a consumer-side filter: session.createConsumer(destination, "region = 'EU' AND amount > 1000") restricts delivery to messages whose headers and properties satisfy an SQL-92 selector expression, so the router component disappears and the broker does the routing. The decision must therefore be expressible over properties - a selector cannot see the body - so the discriminator has to be set as a property (setStringProperty/setIntProperty) by the producer, and the selector is fixed when the consumer is created, meaning a new rule is a new consumer. Use it to keep irrelevant traffic out of the JVM; keep an in-process router when the conditions need the payload.
pitfalls: Selectors see headers and properties only - never the message body - so a body-based route must be promoted to a property at send time or the selector can never match it.
A selector that matches nothing raises no error: the messages simply stay on the queue (or are lost from a non-durable subscription), so unconsumed depth is the metric that reveals it.
Unknown property names evaluate to null and silently never match, so a typo in a property name looks exactly like 'no such messages'.
